findings.title: Opencode bridge dispatches Executor messages to agents without checking the bearer token
findings.description: Authorization is done per branch, not per route. Only the plain operator-text branch (OperatorDispatch.dispatch_user_text) calls Caller.authorize/1. The turn-marker branch first runs dispatch_shadowed_operator_texts/2, which forwards every non-marker trailing user text to OperatorDispatch.send_operator/3 -> AgentChat.send/3. It then opens TurnStream.stream/3, which subscribes the caller to the agent's live AgentPubSub transcript. Neither step checks a token. The Bridge router has only :match, Plug.Parsers and :dispatch, so there is no outer auth plug. The listener is loopback by default, but every agent can reach it: OpenAI-compat sandboxes use --share-net (command_runner.ex:47), and Codex and Claude agents run on the host.
findings.recommendation: Add an auth plug to Aiur.Opencode.Bridge that runs before :dispatch. It should require a TokenRegistry-valid bearer on every /v1/chat/completions request, whatever branch the request takes: turn marker, stream marker, nudge, or operator text. Then remove the per-branch Caller.authorize. Add a regression test: an unauthenticated request whose messages are [user:'do X', user:'__aiur_turn__:t1'] must return 401 and must not call AgentChat.send.

findings.title: OpenAI-compat exec_command sandbox copies GITHUB_TOKEN/GH_TOKEN into every agent command
findings.description: The bwrap sandbox starts with --clearenv. It then re-adds GITHUB_TOKEN and GH_TOKEN, read directly from the daemon's System env. AgentEnvironment.workspace_env marks both names for scrubbing ({name, false}), but agent_environment/2 drops the scrub entries (`_unset -> []`). So nothing overrides the explicit inherited copy. The launcher sources .env into the daemon environment (aiur-engine.sh:805; Init.Dotenv put_env_if_unset), so in the normal configuration the token is present. This breaks the #2356 invariant: 'agents must not inherit the raw GitHub credential'. The existing test sets GH_TOKEN and depends on it reaching the sandbox, so the leak is pinned by a test.
findings.recommendation: Remove GITHUB_TOKEN and GH_TOKEN from @inherited_env_names. Build the sandbox env only from AgentEnvironment.workspace_env, and let the in-sandbox gh guard read the agent token file (AgentGitHubGuard.ensure_agent_token_file) through a read-only bind. Change command_runner_budget_test to provision the token file, and add a test asserting that `env` inside the sandbox contains neither name.

findings.title: `aiur stop` kills live headless agents of every other running aiur instance
findings.description: cmd_stop's 'belt-and-suspenders' sweep iterates every `aiur-*-agents` pidfile in XDG_RUNTIME_DIR (or TMPDIR), not only this instance's, then TERM/KILLs the whole process tree of every recorded pid and deletes the file. Pidfiles are named by the launcher PID (`aiur-${$}-agents`), not the instance key, and nothing checks that the owning instance is down. A second live instance (another project, same user, which the instance-key design explicitly supports) loses its running codex/claude app-servers and its crash-reap backstop file whenever any other project runs `aiur stop` or `aiur restart`. The only pid-reuse guard is a substring match on the command line (`*claude*`, `*codex*`, `*ssh*`), and the file is append-only and never pruned, so a recycled PID now belonging to the operator's own `claude` or `ssh` process also matches. This contradicts the engine's own isolation claims (lines 960-963: 'never another live aiur'; 3418-3423: 'we warn, not reap, to respect the deliberate isolation'). sweep_stale_tmp_artifacts (3395-3405) spares live PID-named files, but this path does not. No test covers it: the sibling-instance test in src/test/aiur_engine_test.exs:2938 checks BEAMs only.
findings.recommendation: Store the run's AIUR_AGENT_TMPFILE in the instance record next to AIUR_RECORD_WORKSPACE_ROOT_FILE and have cmd_stop reap only that file. Alternatively, name pidfiles by instance key (`aiur-<key>-agents`). Sweep another instance's pidfile only after epmd confirms its node is down (probe_named_node_liveness). Record the full `/proc/<pid>/stat` start time, or the exact argv0, as the reuse guard instead of a substring. Add a regression test with two instances' pidfiles.

findings.title: Codex spawns a `ps` process for every streamed JSON-RPC notification
findings.description: Codex.TurnEvents.metadata_from_message/2 rebuilds port metadata from scratch on every call. AppServerPort.port_metadata/1 calls maybe_put_local_process_group, which calls RemoteControl.process_group_for_pid/1. That function runs System.find_executable("ps") and System.cmd(ps, ["-o","pgid=","-p",pid]). When the pgid does not equal the pid, or when ps fails, it retries up to 20 times with Process.sleep(10). TurnLoop.handle_turn_method/5 calls metadata_from_message for every notification that is not turn/completed, and this includes every item/agentMessage/delta and outputDelta. Codex therefore forks and execs `ps` once per streamed delta in the runner's receive loop. After the app-server exits while buffered lines remain, ps fails and each message can stall for about 200 ms (20 x 10 ms plus 20 forks). A remote (ssh) session also runs local `ps` against the ssh pid on every message, because metadata_from_message calls port_metadata(port) without the worker_host.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the process-group metadata once at spawn. AppServerPort.start_port already computes it through notify_process_group_started. Store it in session.metadata, and make metadata_from_message read session.metadata (pass the session, not the port) and attach only per-message usage. Remove the retry/sleep loop from any hot-path caller.

findings.title: Claude permission_mode fails open to bypassPermissions on any unrecognised value
findings.description: Claude.Config.permission_mode/0 maps every value outside ~w(default acceptEdits bypassPermissions) to the most permissive mode. The Ecto schema casts permission_mode as a free string and never validates it, and validate!/0 checks only the command. An operator who writes a stricter mode with a typo ("acceptedits"), or a real Claude CLI mode that the allowlist omits ("plan"), silently gets bypassPermissions on both the app-server path (thread/start permissionMode) and the REPL path (--permission-mode). Nothing is logged or rejected. The Codex equivalent is fail-closed: an invalid approval_policy falls back to "untrusted", and validate_approval_policy/1 returns an explicit error.
findings.recommendation: Add validate_inclusion(:permission_mode, ...) to the schema so a bad value fails config load. Make permission_mode/0 raise, or fall back to the *strictest* mode ("default"), never to bypassPermissions. Keep the explicit bypassPermissions default only for an unset key. Share one 'enum config value' helper with Codex.Config.

findings.title: DisplayTailer truncates transcript bodies mid-codepoint, which produces invalid UTF-8 for the Stream Deck channel and the opencode DB
findings.description: cap_text/2 cuts transcript event bodies and payload.output at a fixed byte offset with binary_part/3 and caps them at 8000 bytes. When byte 8000 falls inside a multi-byte character, the result is invalid UTF-8. Emoji, box-drawing characters, CJK and '…' are routine in tool output and thinking blocks. The capped event goes through on_message to the runner's transcript broadcast. StreamdeckProjection.transcript/2 then passes `body` through unchanged into a Phoenix channel push, which JSON-encodes it. Opencode.Db encodes part data with Jason.encode, which rejects invalid UTF-8, so the row that DisplayTailer exists to paint fails with write_failed. IssueLog.summarize already fixed this exact defect after an invalid byte killed the Stream Deck socket, and its comment describes the failure. agent_chat.ex:64 has the same pattern.
findings.recommendation: Add one UTF-8-safe truncation helper, for example Aiur.Text.truncate_bytes/2, that backs off to a codepoint boundary (or String.slice by graphemes). Use it in DisplayTailer.cap_text, AgentChat and IssueLog. Add a test with a multi-byte character straddling the cap that fails with binary_part.

findings.title: The two JSON-RPC app-server backends (Claude and Codex) duplicate session plumbing that has already diverged on safety properties
findings.description: Claude.CodingAgent calls itself a 'simplified variant of Codex.CodingAgent'. It re-implements, inline, pieces that Codex keeps in AppServerPort, Handshake, Frames, OperatorDelivery and Approvals: workspace validation, port stop, port metadata, initialize/thread/start/turn/start frames, operator delivery and tool-call servicing. The copies no longer match. (a) Workspace check: Codex canonicalises both paths and rejects a symlink escape. Claude only string-prefix-checks the expanded path. (b) stop_port: Codex reaps the descendant tree before Port.close, citing the ~/.codex/state_5.sqlite lock incident. Claude only unregisters and closes, relying on orchestrator teardown. (c) Process group: Codex records agent_process_group_id only after `ps` proves os_pid == pgid, and its comment says callers must never fall back. Claude records os_pid as the group unconditionally, as an integer, where Codex stores a string. (d) Claude registers no PauseContainment, so Adapter.pause_latched? is always false for it. (e) Codex tool calls pass through ToolCallIdentity/ToolCallLedger (idempotency) and deny_for_pause. Claude executes every item/tool/call directly with neither. The request ids 2/3 and the frame shapes are also copied. Aiur.AppServer.OperatorDelivery (used by Claude) and Aiur.Codex.OperatorDelivery (used by Codex) are two different modules with the same short name.
findings.recommendation: Extract one Aiur.AppServer.Session module (workspace validation, spawn, verified process-group metadata, containment registration, stop with tree reap, frame builders, tool-call servicing through the ledger, pause denial). Both backends then plug in only their differences: Codex approvals, sandbox policy and account reads; Claude permissionMode. Decide explicitly, and document, whether Claude needs the tool-call ledger and pause containment, instead of losing them by copy.

findings.title: The Claude REPL paths classify usage-limit exhaustion by substring-matching every key and value of whole records, the over-broad match #2727 removed only from the app-server path
findings.description: usage_limit_exhausted?/1 for a map flattens the payload, keys included (`[key | flatten_values(item)]`), joins every binary, lowercases it and checks for any of 'rate limit', 'rate_limit', 'session limit', 'quota', 'too many requests', 'credit balance'... HookTurn applies it to the entire StopFailure hook payload (`event.raw`). TranscriptTurn applies it to the entire on-disk transcript record that TranscriptTailer.terminal_error_record/1 returns, which includes message content, cwd and gitBranch. Claude.CodingAgent applies it to turn/failed params. A non-limit API failure (500/overloaded) on a branch or workspace named '...quota...' or '...rate_limit...', or with assistant text that mentions rate limits, becomes {:paused, usage_limit_exhausted}. That pause spends no retry, parks the agent and sets reset_at from a regex. The Codex path is gated on willRetry:false plus codexErrorInfo, and #2727 removed free-text matching of provider_error for the Claude app server. The same heuristic survives on both REPL paths.
findings.recommendation: Classify only structured provenance fields: `error` == 'rate_limit' / api_error_status == 429 / isApiErrorMessage plus the error text of the synthetic error message. Never flatten keys or unrelated fields. Share one classifier with the app-server provider_refusal/2 path. Add tests where cwd/gitBranch/assistant text contain 'quota' and the error is a 500. findings.title: ensure_workspace_trusted rewrites the whole ~/.claude.json without a backup, mode preservation or protection against concurrent writers
findings.description: The moduledoc (lines 25 and 66) promises an 'atomic, backup-guarded edit'. The code decodes ~/.claude.json, sets one key and calls Fs.atomic_write(path, Jason.encode!(updated)) without :mode or :fsync. atomic_write takes no backup, and File.write on the temp file leaves it at umask-default permissions, so the rename replaces the user's file with a file whose mode is not the original's. ~/.claude.json holds account metadata. Serialisation covers only aiur's own calls (the Orchestrator handle_call). Every live `claude` process owned by other agents also rewrites ~/.claude.json, so any write they make between aiur's read and rename is lost (lost update on the operator's global Claude config).
findings.recommendation: Preserve the original mode (File.stat, then pass :mode), write a timestamped backup before replacing, and re-read and compare (mtime/size or content hash) just before rename, retrying on change. Better still, write the trust flag through `claude config` or a per-project settings file instead of rewriting the global file. Fix the moduledoc either way.

findings.title: Chat pane drops transcript events whenever a turn is :active but no bridge stream is subscribed
findings.description: SessionWriter skips its SQL write whenever ActiveTurns has any :active turn for the identifier. The intent is to avoid duplicating what the live SSE stream renders. But whether a turn is :active has nothing to do with whether a TurnStream is actually subscribed. TurnStream closes on the watchdog and at every segment boundary without touching ActiveTurns. A failed continuation-marker post only logs. So events published in those windows reach neither the SSE stream nor SQL. The comments claim a SQL fallback, and no code implements it.
findings.recommendation: Base the dedup on actual subscription. Have TurnStream register and unregister its pid in ActiveTurns (the unused register_subscriber/3 already exists for this). SessionWriter should skip only while a live subscriber exists. Buffer events across the segment-close gap, or write them to SQL. Add a test: with an :active turn and no subscriber, a transcript event must be written to SQL.

findings.title: AttachPool.consume runs a multi-second Slot.set_visible inside handle_call; timeouts turn into silent misses
findings.description: consume/2 calls the pool with the default 5 s timeout and turns any exit into :miss. Inside that handle_call, the pool calls Slot.set_visible/3 synchronously, with a 15 s timeout. The pool's own comments say a respawn costs 5-7 s. While it waits, every other pool read (attach_count, visible_count, find_slot_for, snapshot, each with a 1 s timeout) returns 0, :miss or empty. When the consume caller times out it cold-opens a placeholder, and the pool then marks the identifier visible in the slot anyway: two panes, plus a stale reply in the caller's mailbox. do_seed also calls Slot.snapshot on each slot serially inside the pool.
findings.recommendation: Keep AttachPool as pure bookkeeping. The caller should get the slot index from find_slot_for, call Slot.set_visible itself, then cast mark_visible. Alternatively, do the set_visible in a Task and GenServer.reply later. Make the caller's timeout at least the callee's.

findings.title: Slot and HiddenWindow ':failed' are terminal latches; SlotSupervisor docs claim they restart
findings.description: Four paths set `status: :failed` and keep the process alive: serve boot error, attach-pane spawn error, serve EXIT, and HiddenWindow create error. No clause leaves :failed. SlotSupervisor's moduledoc says a :failed slot 'terminates and the supervisor restarts it from scratch'. It does not. acquire_slot_or_grow counts a :failed slot as neither ready nor warming, so the pool grows new slots until max_slots and then returns :no_ready_slot for good. If HiddenWindow fails once at boot (for example tmux is not ready yet), every slot's attach spawn fails with :hidden_window_failed.
findings.recommendation: On failure return `{:stop, {:shutdown, reason}, state}` with backoff, so the :transient restart does its job. Or send :rebuild_now with a bounded retry budget. Have HiddenWindow retry creation. Raise an alert when a slot fails repeatedly. Fix the moduledoc.

findings.title: SlotPolicy never learns a slot died: live_slots/highest_started latch and grow skips holes
findings.description: SlotPolicy subscribes to the slots topic, but it has no clause for {:slot_terminated, idx, pid}, which Slot.terminate broadcasts, and it does not monitor slot pids. live_slots only shrinks when the policy itself drains. So a warm slot that exits permanently is never restarted: next_missing_slot sees it as live. grow_slot always starts `highest + 1`, so it never refills the hole and reaches :at_capacity early. SlotSupervisor.slot_count() (the registry) and SlotPolicy.live_slots can disagree indefinitely.
findings.recommendation: Handle :slot_terminated (or monitor the pids returned by start_slot): remove the index from live_slots, recompute highest_started, and restart it if the index is <= target. Make grow_slot pick the lowest free index.

findings.title: Db.with_transaction commits after an {:error,_} return and ignores COMMIT failure
findings.description: ROLLBACK runs only when fun raises. If fun returns {:error, reason}, as open_turn's `with` does when a part insert fails after the message insert, COMMIT runs and the partial rows persist. open_turn then returns {:error} without recording the turn, so the next event with the same turn_id opens a second assistant message. The COMMIT result is discarded (`_ = Basic.exec(conn, "COMMIT")`). If COMMIT fails (SQLITE_BUSY), the connection closes, an implicit rollback happens, and the caller still sees success. Replay also ignores the root-message insert result and silently counts failed events.
findings.recommendation: Make with_transaction roll back on any non-:ok / {:error,_} return and propagate COMMIT errors. Stop discarding the root insert result during replay. Add Db tests for error-return rollback and COMMIT failure.

findings.title: ToolCallLedger keeps every dynamic tool result forever and fsyncs twice per call through one global GenServer
findings.description: Every Codex dynamic tool call that has a call_id gets a DETS row: {:running} at claim, then {:done, fingerprint, result} with the full normalized result. No code path deletes or compacts entries. init loads the whole table into the GenServer map at boot. Each claim and each complete runs :dets.insert + :dets.sync inside handle_call, and all callers wait with :infinity timeouts. Memory, boot time and file size grow with lifetime tool calls across all tickets. When DETS hits its 2 GB file limit, put fails, claim_new returns {:ledger_unavailable, _}, and every dynamic tool call is refused.
findings.recommendation: Tie ledger entries to the (scope, thread) lifetime: purge a thread's :done entries when its app-server session ends, keeping :uncertain tombstones only while the thread can replay. Or add TTL compaction. Store a result digest plus the spill path instead of full results. Consider one ledger per agent to remove the global serialization.

findings.title: ActiveTurns/TokenRegistry create their named public ETS table lazily from whichever process calls first
findings.description: Every public function calls ensure_table/0. If the table is missing, :ets.new runs in the caller's process, and that process becomes the owner. If the ActiveTurns or TokenRegistry GenServer restarts, the table disappears with it. The next caller then owns the new table: an AgentRunner task, or a Bandit request handler calling TokenRegistry.valid?/1. When that short-lived process exits, the table and every token or active-turn entry vanish again. Result: the bridge answers 401 for all slots, and TurnStream treats live turns as phantoms. Two concurrent callers in that window race :ets.new on a named table (ArgumentError). The same helper appears in 3 more modules outside this unit.
findings.recommendation: Create the tables only in the owning GenServer's init, or use a dedicated table-owner process with an :heir. Readers should return a defined empty result when the table is absent, never create it. Move the 5 copies into one shared helper.

findings.title: Queue-drain pause paths never confirm PauseContainment, so the codex process group is reaped 5s after a pause
findings.description: Every accepted pause request arms PauseContainment (arm_entry schedules {:fallback, id, gen} after grace_ms=5000). If the entry is still :armed when the timer fires, PauseContainment spawns reap_fun (RemoteControl.graceful_kill_process_group) on the agent's recorded process group. The only production caller of PauseContainment.confirm/1 is TurnLoop's primary-turn {:paused, _} branch. The parallel {:paused, _} branch in QueueDrain.run_supported_queue_item_turn (an operator-message or event-digest turn) and the {:pause_agent, id, gen} receive clauses in drain_operator_messages/wait_for_operator_message never confirm. Containment is registered for codex sessions (codex/session_lifecycle.ex:42). Result: pausing a codex agent while it is working a queued operator message (or in the between-turn drain window) turns the pause into a kill of its app-server process group 5s later, raises a false 'Cooperative pause did not contain the agent' fallback event, and the next resume runs a turn on a dead port.
findings.recommendation: Make pause confirmation part of the single turn-settlement path: extract a TurnSettlement.paused(app_session, issue, payload, ctx) used by both TurnLoop and QueueDrain that confirms containment, emits the usage-limit alert, restores delivered items and reports :paused. Also confirm (or skip arming for) pauses received in drain_operator_messages while no turn is running. Add a regression test that drives a {:paused, _} result through run_supported_queue_item_turn with a fake containment server and asserts confirm/1 is called before grace expiry (the test must fail with the confirm removed).

findings.title: QueueDrain hard-matches :ok on orchestrator queue RPCs that TurnLoop documents as fallible (#1238 repeat)
findings.description: The same four orchestrator calls (consume/restore/fail delivered items, settle failure) are handled two different ways. TurnLoop wraps them in best_effort_queue_bookkeeping because 'a briefly overloaded orchestrator queue GenServer answers restore/fail/consume with {:error, :unavailable} / :timeout'. QueueDrain, which runs the identical calls for queued-item turns, uses `:ok =` hard matches at six sites. Its own comment at 758-765 records that issue #1238 was exactly a MatchError from `:ok = restore_delivered_queue_items(...)` on a transient {:error, :unavailable}, converting recovery into an abnormal exit that consumed a retry. The fix was applied to one call site; the pattern remains at the others.
findings.recommendation: Route every queue bookkeeping call through one module (e.g. AgentRunner.QueueBookkeeping) with two explicit policies: best_effort/3 (log + alert-worthy counter) and confirmed/3 (bounded retry, returns {:error, :queue_restore_unconfirmed}). Delete the `:ok =` sites. Add tests where the orchestrator stub returns {:error, :unavailable} for each call from the queue-drain path.

findings.title: Mid-turn operator delivery drops restore/fail results, so a failed send can be consumed as delivered
findings.description: For immediate and safe-checkpoint delivery, CheckpointDelivery claims an item (it becomes :delivered) and hands the backend an on_failure callback whose only action is Orchestrator.restore_queue_item_pending/2 (or mark_queue_item_failed). The return value is never inspected by CheckpointDelivery or by the REPL driver, which calls `on_failure.(reason)` and discards the result. The module comment states the turn-end consume_delivered_queue_items sweep retires anything still :delivered. So when the send fails and the restore RPC returns {:error, :unavailable} (a documented transient reply), the operator's message stays :delivered and is then consumed at turn end without ever reaching the agent. No log line records the failed restore.
findings.recommendation: Make on_failure return a settlement result and have one settle function retry the restore with the same bounded confirm used by TurnLoop.confirm_restore_delivered; if still unconfirmed, emit a ticket-scoped needs-attention alert naming the item id and mark the turn so consume skips that item (consume should only retire items acknowledged via acknowledge_queue_item_delivery).

findings.title: ToolExecutor keys topics, subscriptions and decisions by issue.id while the rest of the runner uses issue.identifier
findings.description: tool_executor.ex has three identity helpers with different precedence: issue_identifier/1 (returns issue.id first, then identifier - the name lies), issue_number_of/1 (number, then identifier) and tracker_issue_id/1 (id then identifier, integers allowed). Agent alert topics, agent event topics, SubscriptionStore attach/add/remove, DecisionStore ticket identity and the coordination key all go through issue_identifier/1 (id-first). Everything else in the runner (TurnAlerts, ModelLabelRefresh, SessionLifecycle alerts, QueueDrain, BootstrapDigest universal subscriptions, CommentContext) uses issue.identifier. For GitHub id == identifier (github/issues.ex:975-976) so it is invisible; for the Linear tracker id is the Linear UUID and identifier is 'ABC-123' (linear/client.ex:465-466), so an agent's own subscriptions attach a different SubscriptionStore than its universal subscriptions, its events publish under ticket.<uuid>.agent.* which identifier-based subscribers never match, and decision requests carry a different ticket identifier than the queue delivery path.
findings.recommendation: Introduce one TicketRef (built once from Issue: tracker_identity, display identifier, tracker id, number) and pass it through the runner; build topics only from TicketRef.topic_key/1. Delete the three ad-hoc helpers. Add a Linear-shaped fixture (id != identifier) to the ToolExecutor tests that asserts the published topic and subscription key equal the identifier-based ones.

findings.title: Help overlay tells the user to press q to leave help, but q shuts down the whole Aiur daemon
findings.description: Input dispatches q to App.quit/1 unconditionally (also while help is visible), and App.quit calls Aiur.Shutdown.shutdown(0), which stops Aiur.Supervisor - every running agent. The help overlay says 'q quit the agent list' and 'Press `?` again or `q` to leave this help screen.' Following the on-screen instruction stops the fleet. The keybind lists have also drifted: the help omits r (remote control), a (attach), O / Shift+Enter (new pane) and the left/right max-agents keys that Input handles, and hardcodes '5 conversation slots' although slot_count = max_vertical_panes*2-1 is configurable.
findings.recommendation: While help_visible? is true route q (and Esc) to toggle_help; require a confirmation (second q within N seconds, or Q) for daemon shutdown. Generate the help keybind list and the footer from one keybinding table that Input.dispatch also uses, and derive the slot count from PaneManager state.

findings.title: Agent bootstrap silently drops missed events and review comments on enqueue or fetch failure
findings.description: The first-turn bootstrap digest (every event missed while the agent was offline, plus unaddressed review comments) is enqueued with a raw GenServer.call to the named Aiur.Orchestrator process with a 5s timeout. On {:error, _} or an exit it logs a Logger.warning and returns :ok, and the cursor is not advanced or retried, so the agent starts work without the review feedback it was dispatched to address. CommentContext does the same for each GitHub fetch (issue comments, open PR lookup, PR review comments, unaddressed threads): any error becomes [] with only a Logger.warning. Without --debug these warnings are written nowhere. The raw call also bypasses the Orchestrator API module (the only such call in the unit).
findings.recommendation: Return a structured bootstrap result {:ok, count} | {:degraded, [source_failures]} and, on degraded, (a) emit a ticket-scoped needs-attention alert naming the failed sources and (b) include a line in the first-turn prompt telling the agent the comment context is incomplete. Retry the enqueue once through an Orchestrator API function instead of a raw tuple call.

findings.title: Ticket-detail refresh loop: every failed detail read broadcasts, the open drawer re-requests, the coordinator re-reads with no backoff
findings.description: Static trace of a feedback loop that runs for as long as the Ticket Context drawer is open on a ticket whose detail read fails. (1) TicketDetailCoordinator.refresh_or_reply starts a new read whenever the entry is not fresh and not inflight, and Policy.fresh?/2 is false for any entry with a failure. The coordinator has no failure backoff, and Failure.retry_after is stored but never read. (2) TaskLifecycle.apply_entry_completion broadcasts {:ticket_detail_updated, state} on every completion, including a failure identical to the previous one. (3) BuildOrderLive routes :ticket_detail_updated to ContextRuntime.refresh_for/2, which rotates the request token. (4) reconcile_scope/2 sees the token change and calls schedule_load, which runs DataSource.load_context. That calls TicketDetailCoordinator.request/1 and returns to step (1). Each pass runs TicketDetail.fetch: a REST conditional read of the issue, then an uncached AiurLinkedPullRequests GraphQL POST, then normalization. A failure that happens after both reads spends a GraphQL request on every pass, at the speed of GitHub's round trip, and at that rate one open drawer can use up the 5,000-point hourly budget. A deterministic trigger exists: any issue body over 16 KiB fails normalization with :validation (see build-order-02). A success does not loop, because the next request finds the entry fresh for freshness_ms.
findings.recommendation: Only broadcast a detail state when its content or health changes (compare with the previous State as TicketHistoryProvider.same_content?/2 does). Give the coordinator a per-entry failure backoff that honours Failure.retry_after (reuse GraphProjection.Policy.retry_due?/2 semantics). Make refresh_for/2 skip rotation when the broadcast generation equals the one already rendered. Add a regression test: keep the drawer subscribed to a reader that always fails, then assert the reader is called a bounded number of times within N broadcasts.

findings.title: Issue bodies larger than 16 KiB make the whole ticket detail fail with :validation instead of being truncated
findings.description: TicketDetail.Normalizer.description/2 passes the raw body to Sanitizer.sanitize/2 with the byte limit. sanitize/2 returns :error when the input is already over the limit, and description/2 maps that to {:error, %Failure{kind: :validation}}. The whole snapshot is then rejected: title, lifecycle and destinations are thrown away along with the body. The limit is capped at TicketDetail.default_max_description_bytes() (16,384), both as the default and as the maximum, so an operator cannot raise it. GitHub bodies can be up to 65,536 characters, and Aiur ticket bodies with workpads regularly pass 16 KiB. The drawer shows 'unavailable' for those tickets, and because the failure is deterministic it drives the loop in build-order-01. The presenter degrades correctly for the same case: TicketContextPresenter.safe_description/1 returns nil on :error. So the two layers treat an oversize body differently.
findings.recommendation: Truncate instead of reject: use Sanitizer.sanitize_projection/3, which already exists and returns {:ok, text, truncated?}, and carry a description_truncated? flag on the Snapshot. Keep :validation for structural faults only.

findings.title: A failed or crashed catalog reconciliation is silently dropped and never retried on a repository without webhooks
findings.description: The catalog is event-sourced from ResourceStore. The GraphQL reconciliation is the only way the store converges on edges that were never delivered. It runs at boot (:reconcile), when an operator runs refresh_catalog, and when the repo's delivery mode is :degraded. When the task returns {:error, reason}, the {ref, result} clause ignores `result`: it clears the inflight marker and stamps last_reconciliation_ms as if the run had succeeded. When the task crashes, the :DOWN clause clears the marker with no log. Nothing records health, raises an alert or schedules a retry. On a repo whose delivery mode is :never_configured (DeliveryMode states: :never_configured | :configured_unproven | :webhook_backed | :degraded), degradation never fires. A boot reconciliation that fails, for example on a missing token, a GraphQL budget hold or a timeout, leaves the catalog on the stale store until an operator happens to press refresh. The #2538 comments say this is the exact failure the design exists to avoid. Failures to start the task are logged only at Logger.warning, which goes nowhere without --debug.
findings.recommendation: Treat the reconciliation as a scope with a health record. Record failure, reason and next_retry_at, schedule a bounded-backoff retry regardless of delivery mode, publish it on the catalog snapshot (for example a :reconciliation_failed diagnostic), and emit an operator alert after N consecutive failures. Stamp last_reconciliation_ms only on success.

findings.title: Reconciliation clears every :sub_issue edge, then re-deposits only the first 100 members of each root
findings.description: deposit_catalog/2 calls ResourceStore.clear(:sub_issue, owner, repo) for the whole repository, then deposits edges from each root's `subIssues(first: 100)` connection. deposit_root/2 ignores pageInfo and totalCount, and never paginates members. For a root with more than 100 sub-issues, every edge past the first page, including edges delivered correctly by webhooks, is deleted from the store on every boot and on every degraded reconciliation. A root whose subIssues connection fails Connection.parse/1 has all its edges cleared and none re-deposited (`_invalid -> :ok`). Queries.ex says outright that 'a root with more than 100 members' exists. After a reconciliation, CatalogStore.member_numbers/1, GraphProjection's member-change debounce, and the catalog member counts all read the truncated store.
findings.recommendation: Clear edges only for a root whose member connection was read completely (has_next? false and length == totalCount). Otherwise leave that root's existing edges and mark it for a paginated selected-root read. Alternatively, clear per parent instead of per repository. Add a test that holds 101 members for one root and asserts no edge is lost after run/1.

findings.title: Due retry combined with max_inflight saturation re-arms a 0 ms timer on every pass (busy loop)
findings.description: Static trace, not reproduced. In handle_info({:graph_projection_due, scope, token}), the entry's timer is set to nil and reconcile/2 runs. On an unchanged fingerprint, reconcile runs reschedule_active_scopes -> restore_selected_retries -> schedule_active_scope. For a watched selected root whose next_retry_at has passed, retry_due? is true, so schedule_scope(state, scope, 0) arms a fresh 0 ms timer with a new token. The handler then calls request_scope. If inflight_by_ref already holds max_inflight reads (default 4), request_scope only defer_scope's the scope into `pending` and does not cancel the new 0 ms timer. The timer fires at once with the matching token, and the cycle repeats. Each pass re-reads configuration, until a read completes and admit_pending runs. A burst of catalog moves that dispatches several selected-root reads (request_changed_selected_roots) while another watched root is in retry backoff is enough to trigger it.

findings.title: Subscription failures in init are swallowed with no log or retry, which latches the event-sourced projections so they stop updating
findings.description: GraphProjection subscribes at init to workflow configuration, to ResourceStore resource types and to delivery-mode events. Each call is wrapped in `rescue _ -> :ok; catch _, _ -> :ok`, and default_resource_subscription/1 swallows errors a second time. The catalog is event-sourced (#2313): if ResourceStore.subscribe_type/1 raises at boot, for example because the store is not yet registered, the projection never receives :github_resource_changed and the catalog stays frozen for the whole daemon lifetime. No log, health bit or retry reports it. The same pattern appears in TicketDetailCoordinator.subscribe_to_configuration/1 and in TicketHistoryProvider init (`_ = safely(options.activity_subscribe_fun)`; `_ = safely(fn -> options.configuration_subscribe_fun.(self()) end)`), which stop following configuration or activity. after_broadcast/2 and publish/2 also swallow failures, and publish/2 silently drops events when Aiur.PubSub is not registered.
findings.recommendation: Treat a failed subscription as a startup failure: crash and let the supervisor retry, since ordering in aiur.ex already starts the dependencies first. If it must be tolerated, record it on the snapshot health (failure: :subscription_unavailable), schedule a bounded retry, and raise an alert. Never swallow without a trace.

findings.title: SubscriptionStore stall recovery reorders buffered events behind newer ones, then drops them as stale (silent event loss)
findings.description: When an enqueue fails transiently, the store holds a stall and buffers later events. resolve_stall/2 advances the cursor to the stalled id and then re-sends the buffered events to its own mailbox with send(self(), ...). Any event that was already in the mailbox behind the {:retry_stalled} message is processed before the re-sent ones. That event is newer, so it advances the cursor past the buffered ids. When the buffered events then arrive, handle_info drops them through the 'event_id <= cursor' branch with no log. The retry itself blocks for up to 1 s in GenServer.call(Aiur.Orchestrator, ..., 1_000), and a slow orchestrator is the usual cause of a stall. So new events are very likely to queue behind the retry exactly when this path runs. The cursor is persisted past the lost ids, so a restart does not replay them either.
findings.recommendation: In resolve_stall/2, drain stalled_buffer inline in order: call process_new_event/4 for each buffered event, and stop and re-buffer at the first new stall. Do not round-trip through the mailbox. Add a test that sends event 102 after {:retry_stalled} while the retry enqueue blocks, and assert that 101 and 102 are both enqueued in order.

findings.title: Claims.renew revives an expired owner after a successor claimed, producing two live owners
findings.description: The moduledoc says two live owners cannot happen because the takeover check runs under the lock. do_claim/3 only refuses when a *live* owner exists, and it never demotes the expired owner's entry. do_renew/3 then calls touch/5 with the entry's existing role and no liveness or ownership check. Sequence: A's lease lapses (host suspended or process stopped for more than 10 min). B claims. A resumes and renews, through the Principal timer or the executor-wait CLI. A becomes a live 'owner' next to B. do_record_acknowledgement/4 then accepts acks from whichever owner Map.values happens to list first and refuses the other. owner/1 and the roster report an arbitrary one of the two.
findings.recommendation: In do_claim, when taking over from an expired owner, demote that entry to 'expired' or 'observer' in the same write. In do_renew, refuse to renew role 'owner' when the lease has lapsed and another live owner exists, returning {:error, {:held_by, other}}. Add the renew-after-takeover test.

findings.title: GithubCIPoller.poll runs synchronously inside the Orchestrator GenServer (the #1837 blocking pattern the comment poller was moved away from)
findings.description: The dispatcher made the comment poll async because the Orchestrator was captured blocked in its Task.async_stream fan-out. The very next line calls CiLifecycle.poll_github_ci, which calls GithubCIPoller.poll synchronously in the Orchestrator process. The fan-out uses max_concurrency 4 and a 60 s timeout per target, so a slow GitHub can hold the Orchestrator for ceil(N/4)*60 s. On the REST fallback path each target makes up to five sequential requests: the branch PR lookup, ensure_pull_request_base (which may PATCH), two commit-status reads, and a second PR lookup for the recheck. If Aiur.TaskSupervisor is not registered, the poller toggles trap_exit on the Orchestrator itself. Unlike the comments poller, it exposes no max_duration_ms for callers to bound it. While the Orchestrator is blocked, SubscriptionStore's 1 s enqueue calls time out, which feeds finding 01.
findings.recommendation: Run the CI poll the same way as the comment poll: spawn an owned task and deliver the result as a message ({:github_ci_polled, ...}) that the Orchestrator folds in. Add GithubCIPoller.max_duration_ms/2 as the comments poller does, and delete the trap_exit fallback.

findings.title: Every daemon restart can raise a false 'webhook.never_delivered' needs-attention alert: mode state is memory-only and the check ignores elapsed time
findings.description: ModeRegistry keeps repo modes and the 'observed' novelty map in process memory only, so every restart reseeds configured repos as :configured_unproven with delivery_count 0. The first view-state head check after boot records the unchanged open-issue head as novel activity, because 'observed' is empty. Filtered publishes are also counted. The :configured_unproven sweep clause then alerts as soon as there is any activity and zero deliveries. It never compares against threshold_ms, even though the clause takes it as a parameter. With the 60 s default sweep, any repo that receives no delivery in its first minute after boot raises: 'This is a setup that has never worked'. The registry's own comments call false alerts the thing that makes operators stop reading.
findings.recommendation: Require the silence threshold to have elapsed since the registry booted (or since activity began) before reporting :never_delivered. Also persist per-repo delivery_count and last_delivery_at (a small JSON file under the runtime state dir, as DeliveryLog does) so a proven repo stays proven across restarts. Add a test: fresh registry, activity at t=10s, sweep at t=60s, refute the never_delivered alert.

findings.title: Webhook-published comment events always carry review_decision=nil, so the rework gate is disabled whenever the webhook wins the dedup race
findings.description: The normalizer's own comment documents a live behavioural divergence. On an APPROVED PR, the poller's GraphQL batch publishes review_decision 'APPROVED' and the rework gate suppresses rework. The webhook publishes nil, which routes the ticket to rework, for the same GitHub event. The delivery is free and arrives first, and Publisher's durable resource dedup lets the first producer's shape win. So on any webhook-backed repo the ReviewFreshness gate is inert for almost every comment. The two-producer 'one shape' contract is broken, and the break is recorded only in a code comment.
findings.recommendation: Enrich webhook comment events with review_decision before publishing. The delivery task already runs off the request path, so a one-field GraphQL read, or a read of the DeliveredPullRequest/PollSnapshots state, is affordable there. Alternatively, have the rework gate re-read reviewDecision when the event field is nil instead of failing open. Add an equivalence test asserting both producers yield the same routing for an APPROVED PR.

findings.title: CODEOWNERS team-resolution failure silently drops the team from dispatch trust, contradicting the moduledoc, and can revoke running agents
findings.description: The moduledoc promises that resolution failures preserve the previous allowlist. The code does not. When GET /orgs/{org}/teams/{team}/members fails, resolve_team logs a warning and returns [], so the refreshed allowlist and state.codeowners lose every member of that team. When tracker.github.allowed_users is unset, Config.allowed_users/0 falls back to codeowners_snapshot. DispatchAuthorization then evaluates membership against the CURRENT allowlist on every call, including cached decisions. A label applier or prior triager who was only trusted through the team becomes a non-member, so the issue is denied (not deferred). Reconciler terminates running agents on a non-deferred denial. The only trace is Logger.warning, which is written nowhere without --debug. The state lasts until the next hourly refresh.
findings.recommendation: Carry per-token resolution state. On a failed team lookup, keep that team's previously resolved members and mark the snapshot degraded. Raise a needs_attention alert (github.codeowners.team_unresolved) rather than Logger.warning. Separately, have DispatchAuthorization treat a degraded or unavailable CODEOWNERS-derived allowlist as {:deferred, :allowlist_unavailable}, never as a membership verdict.

findings.title: A busy or absent CodeOwners GenServer turns allowed_users into []: every dispatch is denied and running agents can be revoked
findings.description: CodeOwners.do_refresh makes synchronous, possibly paginated GitHub calls (Client.fetch_team_members, which goes through Budget admission and a 30s request deadline) inside handle_continue and handle_info(:refresh_tick). While it runs, every GenServer.call waits in the mailbox. That includes allowed?/2, which the events sanitizer calls per comment, and codeowners_snapshot/1, which GitHub.Config calls per dispatch authorization. Config.codeowners_users/0 catches the resulting exit (5s default call timeout) or a missing process and returns []. [] is a specific answer ("nobody is allowed"), not "unavailable". It feeds the same denial-then-revocation chain as github-a-01. The sanitizer treats the same exit as untrusted and drops comment bodies. A config reader that makes a blocking GenServer call is also a layering inversion (GitHub.Config -> CodeOwners -> GitHub.Config).
findings.recommendation: Publish the resolved allowlist and codeowners set to ETS or :persistent_term and read them without a call. Run team resolution in a Task and swap the result in on completion. Make Config.allowed_users return {:ok, list} | :unavailable so DispatchAuthorization defers instead of denying. Remove the GenServer dependency from the config module.

findings.title: fetch_classified_issue_comments reads only page 1 (oldest 100): agents silently lose the newest PR conversation comments
findings.description: Two readers of the same /issues/{n}/comments endpoint handle pagination in opposite ways. fetch_issue_comments_conditional drains every page, and its own comment explains that the list is oldest-first, so new comments land on the LAST page. fetch_classified_issue_comments issues one request with per_page=100 through Transport.fetch_json_list. findings.title: CODEOWNERS is parsed by two modules with different grammars, and team members are fetched by two implementations
findings.description: Aiur.GitHub.CodeOwners (the allowlist GenServer) and Aiur.Codeowners (comment classification) both read and tokenise the CODEOWNERS file, and the grammars differ. Aiur.Codeowners drops trailing inline # comments (take_while not "#") and ignores rules with ! or [ patterns. GitHub.CodeOwners requires every token after the pattern to contain "@", so any line with a trailing comment ("* @alice # lead") makes the WHOLE file {:unparseable, line}. That is degraded mode: the allowlist becomes trusted accounts only and a warning alert fires. The same file is thus valid for comment classification and invalid for comment trust. Team expansion is also duplicated: GitHub.CodeOwners goes through Client -> Teams (paginated), while Aiur.Codeowners has its own unpaginated copy, which its own comment admits.
findings.recommendation: Make one CODEOWNERS parser (a pure module returning rules plus diagnostics) the source for both the allowlist and ownership classification. Delete the unpaginated team fetch in Aiur.Codeowners and use Teams. Rename to make the split obvious (e.g. Aiur.GitHub.CodeOwners.Allowlist vs Aiur.GitHub.CodeOwners.Ownership).

findings.title: Order-sensitive store keys have five writers with three staleness policies; one is check-then-act and three are unguarded
findings.description: The store says fetch-then-put loses writes and that the 2-arity update_resource/3 is the safe way to make a conditional write; the webhook Deposit does its regression check inside the swap. Issues.put_issue_resource does the same check outside the swap (fetch, compare, then put_resource), which is the check-then-act the store forbids, and its comment admits it must mirror Deposit by hand. ResourceFetch.store (the strict read HumanReviewGate uses for :branch_pull_request), WriteThrough.deposit (:issue, :pull_request) and Build Order reconciliation (:sub_issue) call put_resource with no regression check, although every one of these types is in @order_sensitive_types. A webhook body that lands during the fetch round trip is overwritten by the older fetched body, and fetched_at_ms is stamped 'now', so freshness-bounded readers are served the rollback.
findings.recommendation: Add one store primitive, ResourceStore.deposit_unless_older(key, body, opts), built on the 2-arity update_resource/3 and a single regression?/2 predicate moved from Deposit into the store. Route Issues.put_issue_resource, ResourceFetch.store, WriteThrough.deposit, reconciliation and Deposit through it. Delete Issues.regression?/2.

findings.title: Review-thread reply mutation is retried after ambiguous failures and can post the reply twice
findings.description: do_reply_to_review_thread/7 retries addPullRequestReviewThreadReply whenever Errors.retryable_github_error?/1 is true. That includes a transport deadline (Transport turns {:error, :fetch_deadline_exceeded} into {:github, :transport, ...}) and every 5xx. In both cases GitHub may already have applied the mutation. The module doc claims 'a successful mutation is never posted twice', but a mutation whose response was lost is posted again. The read cache in the same unit treats any answered write, including a 500, as possibly applied. The later verification passes on the duplicate, because the latest comment's body equals the reply body.
findings.recommendation: Retry a mutation only for errors that prove the request never reached GitHub (local hold, broker timeout, DNS failure, connection refused). For ambiguous failures (deadline, closed socket, 5xx), re-read the thread with the existing verify path first and re-post only if the reply is absent. Add a test whose request_fun applies the mutation and then answers {:error, :fetch_deadline_exceeded}.

findings.title: Quota is a 1,380-line GenServer on every request's path that scans the filesystem and emits alerts in its callbacks
findings.description: Every GitHub request makes a synchronous Quota.preflight GenServer.call (default 5 s timeout) and a cast observe. The same process also appends the durable request log, writes or removes hold files on every observed response, reads and parses every workspace's agent-requests.tsv (and .1) during snapshot, globs the workspace root for stale-broker markers on every snapshot and every refresh, emits alerts from inside a read (snapshot) call, and messages the Orchestrator. QuotaHistory calls snapshot every 30 s, and the dashboard and CLI call it too. While a snapshot reads files, preflight calls queue behind it; if one exceeds 5 s the catch returns :ok and the request goes out unmetered, so quota gating fails open without a signal. sync_hold_file/3 also calls File.rm on every observed response whose window is not exhausted. 914 code lines.
findings.recommendation: Split into: (1) QuotaWindows, holding windows and backoffs in ETS so preflight and dispatch_status are ETS reads, not calls; (2) QuotaAttribution, the observation ring plus ranking and reconciliation (summarize_*, coverage/3 and reconciliation/1 are already pure); (3) AgentShellLogReader, a separate periodic process that ingests agent-requests.tsv and stale-broker markers and emits their alerts; (4) a hold-file writer that acts only on window-state transitions; (5) a RequestLog writer process that owns its io_device. Replace the Orchestrator send with a PubSub event.

findings.title: One failed follow-up append latches the DecisionStore read-only until restart, with no alert, and halts fleet dispatch
findings.description: persist_revision_follow_up_required and ensure_superseded_revision_follow_ups route an append error to fatal_lifecycle_append_failed, which sets `writable?: false` and a health tuple, with only Logger.error (not written anywhere without --debug). No Alerts call, no retry, and nothing in the module ever sets writable? back to true (only boot does). The new health `{:lifecycle_append_failed, type, reason}` is not `readable?`, so blocked_ticket_ids/0 answers {:error, :store_unavailable} and the Orchestrator dispatcher holds EVERY new dispatch (fail-closed gate). The only exit is a daemon restart. Other lifecycle append failures in the same module take a different path (recover_background_append: needs-attention alert plus bounded retry). The same fault has two policies, and the stricter one is the silent one.
findings.recommendation: Route follow-up append failures through recover_background_append (alert + bounded retry keyed by action_id) like every other lifecycle append. If a truly fatal state is needed, emit a needs-attention alert that names the cause, keep the store readable (blocked_ticket_ids can still serve the in-memory projection), and add an explicit recovery path (retry the append on the next reconcile tick, or an operator RPC) instead of requiring a restart.

findings.title: A derived-projection write failure makes the store read-only and silently suppresses publication of already-durable events
findings.description: decisions.json is a derived cache of the audit log (the ndjson is authoritative, per the module's own alert text). Yet repair_projection runs after EVERY accepted mutation and, on any write error, flips `writable?: false` / `health: {:repair, reason}` until restart. That health is not readable?, so dispatch is held fleet-wide (same path as loose-1-02). Worse, the event that triggered the failed write is already appended and fsynced, but repair_and_notify_lifecycle and persist_enrichment only notify `if next_state.writable?`. The answer, dismissal or delivery event is durable yet never published to the Exchange or PubSub, and the Executor escalation is never resolved. No retry covers this. The request path (persist_and_notify) does notify unconditionally, so the three write paths already disagree.
findings.recommendation: Treat decisions.json as a best-effort cache: on a write failure, alert and retry on a timer, but stay writable because the ndjson is the source of truth. Always publish an event once it is durable (publication failure is a separate, retryable concern). Put the three persist paths on one "apply + notify" helper so the policy exists once.

findings.title: `aiur status` serially aggregates ~10 blocking subsystem reads whose worst-case timeouts sum far past the 10s launcher budget
findings.description: After the (read-model backed, 5s-bounded) fleet view, print_status_report calls in sequence: ExecutorListener.bindings, ExecutorWakeInbox.stats (GenServer.call, default 5s), CodeOwners.trust_snapshot (GenServer.call, default 5s), Config.settings!, SupervisionHealth.status (GenServer.call 5s, which also re-evaluates the tree and may emit alerts), CiReadiness.cached_result, BuildGate.status (python3 + sh spawns with no timeout), RepoBase.status (5s), and Asks.open, which opens an EXCLUSIVE SQLite transaction with a 30s busy_timeout and replays the whole asks log. The code's own comments cite #1684, #1837 and #2329 as incidents of exactly this shape (a status command stalled behind one blocked dependency). Each fix moved one read off a mailbox; the aggregation pattern remained.
findings.recommendation: Have each owning process publish its status section into the same SnapshotStore read model the fleet view uses (with observed_at), so `status` performs zero synchronous cross-process calls. Until then, run the section probes concurrently under one shared deadline (Task.async_stream with timeout) and render a timed-out section as `UNAVAILABLE (timed out)` rather than stalling the whole command.

findings.title: BuildGate.status spawns unbounded external processes and writes /tmp files inside the Orchestrator dispatch admission path
findings.description: Dispatcher.admission_probes (run by maybe_choose_under_load inside the Orchestrator GenServer on each dispatch cycle) calls DispatchPolicy.read_build_status -> BuildGate.status. On Linux that writes a manifest to System.tmp_dir!, runs `python3 build_gate_holder.py --scan-locks-manifest` via System.cmd with no timeout, then spawns `sh -c 'kill -0 -PGID'` once per holder and one more python3 per `.hold-timeout` marker. A hung python (e.g. blocked lock/NFS) wedges the orchestrator mailbox indefinitely, the failure class behind #1837/#2137. The same scan also runs from BuildGateHoldMonitor (30s), RunTelemetry.Sampler and `aiur status`, so three independent pollers repeat it.
findings.recommendation: Make BuildGateHoldMonitor the single scanner: run the python scan through a Port with a hard timeout and kill-on-timeout (Aiur.Git.run_bounded_cmd already implements this), publish the result plus observed_at to ETS/persistent_term, and have admission, telemetry and the CLI read the cached snapshot with its age. Replace per-holder `sh kill -0` with a /proc check through ProcessIdentity. Pass the manifest over stdin instead of /tmp.

findings.title: ExecutorEvents treats an unreadable subscription file as empty, then overwrites it; all writers race without a lock
findings.description: subscription_state/0 maps every JsonStore.read error (corrupt JSON, EACCES, EMFILE) to `%{"subscribed_to" => [], "last_seen_event_id" => nil}` with no log or alert. The next subscribe/unsubscribe/advance_cursor/reconcile_subscriptions persists that empty state over the file, losing every manual subscription and resetting the cursor, so the next listen replays the whole journal. Separately, four writers do unlocked read-modify-write of the same file from different processes (CLI RPC subscribe/unsubscribe, the listen loop's advance_cursor per delivered event, ExecutorBindings.reconcile in the daemon), so concurrent writes lose updates (a cursor advance can erase a new subscription, or a reconcile can move the cursor backwards).
findings.recommendation: Return {:error, _} for anything but :enoent, refuse to persist over an unreadable file, and emit a needs_attention alert. Serialize all subscription/cursor mutations through one owner process (or a file lock like Asks.Store.with_lock) instead of per-caller RMW.

findings.title: ExecutorEvents replays the entire, never-compacted journal on every dedup lookup, inside DecisionStore; one corrupt line latches all Command notifications
findings.description: publish_deferred/2, ensure_requested/1 and reconcile_requested/1 each call journal_events/0, which reads and decodes the whole append-only journal. Nothing compacts it (only IdGenerator also scans it). publish_deferred runs synchronously from DecisionStore.notify_lifecycle, so every deferral costs O(journal) file I/O on the DecisionStore process. If any line is corrupt, journal_events returns {:error, {:corrupt, ...}} and emits a needs_attention alert on every call; publish_deferred and ensure_requested then fail forever until an operator hand-repairs the file. DecisionStore's notify_deferred_executor only logs a warning on failure, with no retry (unlike requested notifications), so a deferred Command can silently never reach the Executor.
findings.recommendation: Maintain an in-memory index {topic, decision_id, version} -> event_id in the owning process (built once at boot) instead of replaying per call; add retention/compaction for the journal; skip-and-quarantine a corrupt line rather than failing all lookups; give deferred notifications the same retry schedule requested notifications have.

findings.title: RepoBase latches an {:error, _} prewarm phase forever under the default config (poll_seconds: 0); warm base is never rebuilt
findings.description: The only production entry into RepoBase is refresh_for_dispatch/0 (dispatcher.ex:2233). Its state machine returns an error phase unchanged, so once one build/fetch/probe fails the phase stays {:error, _}. The only other exits from an error phase are handle_info(:poll) and handle_cast(:refresh_async). :poll is scheduled only when prewarm.poll_seconds > 0 and the schema default is 0 (also written by `aiur init`), and refresh_async/0 has zero callers in src/lib. The comment on probe_failed/2 ('later scheduled refreshes can retry the probe/build') is therefore false for default installs. The failure is reported only through Logger.warning in the dispatcher, and LogFile removes every log handler unless --debug is set, so every later dispatch cold-clones and recompiles with no visible signal until the daemon restarts.
findings.recommendation: Make the error phase retryable inside RepoBase itself. Record failed_at and a backoff attempt count on build_done/probe failure, and have dispatch_refresh_state restart start_build/4 once the backoff has elapsed, whatever poll_seconds is set to. Emit a durable attention alert (system.prewarm.base_unavailable, plus .resolved on :ready) from a Task, not only a Logger line. Delete refresh_async/0 and handle_cast(:refresh_async) or wire them to a real caller.

findings.title: AlertLedger compaction has no hysteresis: at the 8 MiB cap every append re-reads, re-decodes and fsync-rewrites the whole ledger in the caller; lock timeouts drop alerts silently
findings.description: append_locked/3 compacts whenever size + new_entry > max_bytes. compact_file/3 keeps the newest entry, the active attention entries, and then history until the next entry would not fit (select_history/3 halts on the first entry that does not fit). The file after compaction therefore sits within one entry of max_bytes. The next append of a similar-sized entry exceeds the cap again and triggers another full compaction: File.stream! of about 8 MiB, JSON-decoding every line, active-set reduction, and Fs.atomic_write with fsync. At steady state this happens on nearly every alert. It runs in whichever process emits the alert (the orchestrator's handle_info among them) while holding the :global append lock, whose timeout is 1 s. A concurrent appender that times out gets {:error, :lock_timeout}, and Alerts.write_alert_ledger_entry/3 discards the return value, so the alert never reaches the AlertFeed, which reads this ledger. The ledger has been durable across restarts since #2722, so it will reach the cap.
findings.recommendation: Compact to a low-water mark (for example 60% of max_bytes) so that one compaction pays for many appends. Move ledger writes behind a single-writer process that emitters cast to, as RecentMergeStore does, so emitters never block on disk. Count and surface append failures (a health field plus a rate-limited alert) instead of discarding them.

findings.title: WorkflowStore config-reload failures are reported only via Logger.error, which writes nowhere without --debug, so a broken config edit is silently ignored
findings.description: When an operator edits .aiur/config (or the prompt/hooks files) and the result fails to parse or validate, the store keeps the last good workflow and records failed_stamp. The only signal is log_reload_error/2 → Logger.error. LogFile.configure/0 removes both the aiur file handler and the default console handler unless AIUR_DEBUG is set, so the message goes nowhere. Nothing reads failed_stamp: it is not exposed through a health/status call and no alert is emitted. The operator believes the new config is live while the daemon runs the old one. This is the 'silent refusal' bug family.
findings.recommendation: Add WorkflowStore.health/0 returning {:ok | {:reload_failed, reason, since}} and render it in `aiur status` and the dashboard. Emit `system.config.reload_failed` (needs_attention) once per failing stamp and `.resolved` on the next good load, dispatched from a Task so the store never blocks on the alert pipeline.

findings.title: IssueLog.record_event/3 is documented as a non-blocking cast but makes a synchronous GenServer.call per event from the publisher, and a timeout silently drops the event marker
findings.description: The doc says 'Async cast — never blocks the publisher.' In fact record_event → writer_for_path → writer_path → GenServer.call(pid, :path, 1_000) for every ticket-scoped publish. Events.Publisher.publish runs in the caller's process: the orchestrator, alert emitters and the subscription store. Each publish therefore waits on the per-ticket writer, whose mailbox also receives every transcript event for that agent. On a 1 s timeout, writer_path returns nil, writer_for_path returns [], and record_event returns :ok without writing or logging anything. The [event:*] rows are what IssueLog.event_history/2 replays, and BootstrapDigest uses that replay to tell a resumed agent which events it missed, so a dropped marker is a missed event delivery.
findings.recommendation: Store the writer's path as the Registry value when registering (Registry.register(..., key, path)) so the lookup is a pure ETS read. The key already encodes repository scope and identifier, so the path check becomes a value comparison with no call. Then use send/2. When no writer exists, append the marker directly to the .events.log file, or count the drop, rather than returning :ok.

findings.title: ProcessReaper's pid-reuse guard needs /proc; on macOS (published darwin-arm64 target) every comm-guarded agent/serve pid is classified gone and never killed
findings.description: The moduledoc calls the registry 'the correctness-critical kill path' so that no agent survives an aiur exit. read_cmdline/1 reads /proc/<pid>/cmdline. On a host without /proc the read fails, and cmdline_guard/3 maps any read failure to :skip_gone ('the process is already gone'), which is a silent no-op. The opencode serve (comm: "opencode"), claude REPL (comm: "claude") and codex app-server (comm: reaper_comm) registrations all carry :comm, so on darwin-arm64, which is in PUBLISH_TARGETS, none of them is reaped by this layer. Only pane refs and comm-less pids are killed. The other layers (per-backend reapers, launcher watchdog) are the only protection left, and the launcher's pidfile reaper also guards on the recorded comm.
findings.recommendation: Put a platform probe behind Aiur.Os: /proc/<pid>/cmdline on Linux, and `ps -o command= -p <pid>` on Darwin. Tell 'unreadable' apart from 'gone' with kill -0 before choosing :skip_gone, and log skip_gone at warning when the pid is still alive. Add a Darwin case to the tests using the injectable :cmdline_reader.

findings.title: TestReset re-derives the workspace path as <root>/<id> but Workspace.Layout places GitHub workspaces at <root>/<owner>/<repo>/<id>; `aiur --test` leaves the stale workspace behind

Workspace.Layout.issue_workspace_path/2 inserts the owner/repo segment whenever the tracker is GitHub (or a Linear project_slug) and the root does not already end in that segment. The reset therefore removes a path that does not exist ('workspace already clean') and leaves the real workspace with the previous run's dirty tree, which is the exact symptom the code comment says this step exists to prevent. The test suite's own fixture uses the nested shape (`/tmp/aiur-workspaces/repo/334`, test_reset_test.exs:129). Sanitization also differs: Paths.sanitize(to_string(id)) here, Paths.sanitize(identifier, "issue") in Layout. print_plan also claims the step 'fans across worker.ssh_hosts', but the implementation is a local File.rm_rf only. The layout logic was copied and has since diverged.
findings.recommendation: Call Aiur.Workspace.workspace_path_under(root, id), the public helper that exists for this purpose, inside the existing rescue, or call Workspace.remove_issue_workspaces/1 when config loads. Correct the plan text, or implement the ssh fan-out.

findings.title: BuildGateHoldMonitor.init returns {:ignore, state}; documented build-gate opt-out crashes daemon boot
findings.description: When BuildGate.enabled?/0 is false, init/1 returns the tuple {:ignore, %State{}}. gen_server only accepts the bare atom `ignore`; any other term is exit({bad_return_value, Else}), so start_link returns an error, the child fails to start, and Aiur.Supervisor (and the whole application) fails to boot. BuildGate.enabled? is false exactly for the documented explicit opt-out (configuration.md:369: max_concurrent_builds: 0, build_start_stagger_seconds: 0, min_free_memory_mb omitted). Config is readable at this point (Workflow.current_with_cache_identity/0 falls back to Workflow.load/0 before WorkflowStore starts), so the fail-open `true` fallback does not mask it. Aiur.SaturationSentinel has the identical bug for `agent.saturation_log_enabled: false`. The test file (test/aiur/build_gate_hold_monitor_test.exs, 122 lines) only exercises evaluate/2 and never starts the process with the gate disabled.
findings.recommendation: Return the bare `:ignore` in both modules. Add a test per module that starts it via start_supervised with the gate/sentinel disabled and asserts `:ignore` (fails today with bad_return_value). Grep the tree for `{:ignore,` as a lint rule.

findings.title: :global.trans lock id {__MODULE__, path} provides no mutual exclusion; model-usage.json and ci-approvals.json read-modify-writes race
findings.description: :global.trans/2 takes {ResourceId, LockRequesterId} and grants the lock to every caller that presents the same requester id. ModelAvailability.observe/3 and CIApprovalStore.journal_base_repair/3 use {__MODULE__, path}: resource = the module, requester = the path, so every caller on the same file is admitted concurrently and the load->merge->write sequence is unprotected. ModelAvailability.observe is called from every agent runner process (codex/session_lifecycle.ex:63 on every rate-limit notification, agent_runner/message_handler.ex:80, agent_runner/turn_alerts.ex:24 via mark_limited), so concurrent writes are routine; a lost update drops another backend's limit entry, making an exhausted backend read as available to CodingAgent.select_for_dispatch and RateLimitFallback. The codebase already documents and fixed this exact inversion in two places, so the logic has diverged. Two more sites outside this unit use the same shape.
findings.recommendation: Introduce one helper (e.g. Aiur.FileLock.with_lock(path, fun) = :global.trans({{:aiur_file, path}, self()}, fun, [node()])) and use it at all six sites; add a concurrency test that runs two observe/3 calls for different backends in parallel with a slowed writer and asserts both entries survive (fails today). Longer term, serialize each ledger through a single owning process instead of global locks.

findings.title: CIApprovalStore.save/3 overwrites the whole file without any lock and can erase a journaled :repairing marker
findings.description: journal_base_repair/3 is documented as strict ('the caller must not mutate GitHub unless the :repairing marker is on disk') and does a locked read-modify-write of all three sections. save/3, called from the Orchestrator's CI lifecycle, writes all three sections from the caller's in-memory copy with no lock and no re-read. A save that races (or simply follows with a stale in-memory map) replaces base_repair_invalidations with an older value, so the marker that justified a GitHub mutation disappears; after a restart the repair is invisible. save/3 also swallows every failure with rescue -> Logger.warning.
findings.recommendation: Make one owner process for the file (or at minimum route save/3 through the same corrected lock and merge base_repair_invalidations from disk rather than from the caller). Give each section its own update function (update_approved_heads/1 etc.) so no caller writes fields it does not own.

findings.title: ExecutorWakeInbox latches on one invalid journal line: boot stops, flush retries forever silently, trim never runs
findings.description: DecisionLog.replay/2 never skips past the first line the validator rejects and returns {:ok, prefix, corruption}. Every inbox path treats corruption as fatal or ignores it: init/1 returns {:stop, corruption} (ExecutorWakeInbox is an always-on child of the flat :rest_for_one tree, so the daemon does not boot); flush_pending/1 on error just re-arms the debounce timer with no log or alert, forever; trim_consumed/1 swallows the error so the #1661 size bound stops applying; wait/stats return {:error, corruption} to every consumer. validate_record/1 is strict (integer wake_id, integer-or-nil event_id, binary topic), so a projection shape change or one byte-rotted line is enough. There is no repair or quarantine path in the module, unlike DecisionProjection.reduce_checked/1.
findings.recommendation: Adopt the reduce_checked pattern: keep the valid prefix, move the corrupt tail to a quarantine file, emit a needs-attention alert (e.g. executor.wakes.corrupt), and continue. Log and alert when a flush fails more than N times instead of re-arming silently. Never return {:stop, _} from init for data corruption.

findings.title: Wake records are dropped with only Logger.error while acknowledge_as holds the inbox inside a cross-process lock
findings.description: handle_call({:acknowledge_as, ...}) calls Executor.Claims.record_acknowledgement/2 (a GenServer call with a 30s call timeout and a 5s file-lock retry) inside the inbox's own callback, then replays and rewrites the journal. While that runs, ExecutorListener.deliver/2 calls ExecutorWakeInbox.enqueue/2 with the default 5s GenServer.call timeout. The exit is caught in process_event/2 and only logged; the listener advances its replay watermark only for executor.* topics, so a non-executor wake that timed out is never retried. #2600 fixed the symptom on the acknowledge path by raising its call budget (claim_call_timeout_ms = max(lock, call) + 30_000) but left enqueue at 5s: the 'fix by raising a limit' family.
findings.recommendation: Do the lease check outside the inbox process (caller asks Claims, then sends a cheap advance message), or make enqueue a cast into the pending map (already persisted) so it never blocks. Any delivery failure must be retried from a durable source or raise an alert, not just a log line.

findings.title: argv round-trip via AIUR_ARGV_FILE splits arguments on newlines and drops empty arguments
findings.description: write_argv writes one argument per line. Aiur.CLI.argv_from_file splits on "\n" and rejects "". So an argument that contains a newline becomes several argv entries, and an empty argument disappears. This breaks the documented `aiur ask <title> --body <text>`: evaluate_ask_create requires `[title] <- positional`, so a multi-line body turns into extra positionals and returns a generic usage error. The same happens to `aiur findings --record <json>` with pretty-printed JSON and to any run argument with a newline. The one-shot paths exec the release (run_version, run_init, run_findings, run_asks), so the argv tempfile is never removed. The file can hold `--body` text and stays in TMPDIR until the 24h sweep.
findings.recommendation: Write NUL-delimited argv (`printf '%s\0'`) and split on <<0>> without dropping empties, or base64-encode each line. Delete the file in argv_from_file after reading it. Add an ExUnit case that sends a multi-line --body through the engine.

findings.title: Two diverged tmux confs: the shipped conf has the documented Ctrl+C bug, the verify harness tests the unshipped copy, and the Ctrl+C bridge is never wired
findings.description: The engine loads only share/aiur.tmux.conf (resolve_tmux_conf falls back to `$engine_dir/../share/aiur.tmux.conf`, and aiur.js sets the same path). aiurdev uses the same engine and does not set AIUR_TMUX_CONF, so dev and product both load share/. That file (86 lines) still uses the `h="#{@aiur_ctrlc}"; $h` form that verify-ctrlc-binding.sh describes as silently falling through to raw kill-pane. It also lacks the C-q hide binding and the `terminal-features *:sync` line, both of which exist only in scripts/aiur.tmux.conf (109 lines), which no launcher loads. verify-ctrlc-binding.sh sources scripts/aiur.tmux.conf, so it passes against a file nobody runs. Ctrl+C on a chat pane therefore always raw-kills the pane, the outcome the harness says drops a queued Executor message.

Ship the helper under libexec/ and have PaneManager.Anchor set `@aiur_ctrlc` next to `@aiur_control_url`. Point verify-ctrlc-binding.sh at the shipped conf and add it to the CI `workflow security`/lint job. If the feature is abandoned, delete the helper, the dashboard endpoint and the harness.

findings.title: Project-root and config discovery diverge between the engine (walks up from cwd) and Elixir (cwd, then HOME)
findings.description: The engine walks up from $PWD to the first directory with .aiur/config, stopping at $HOME, and uses it for the instance key. The walk is implemented three times (aiur_project_root, aiur_project_root_source, legacy_config_path), and the home_real canonicalisation is repeated at lines 100, 231 and 250. Workflow.config_path_candidates checks only `cwd/.aiur/config`, then `~/.aiur/config`. The pane launcher runs the BEAM with `cd $PWD`. So `aiur` started from repo/src is keyed and controlled as the repo instance, but the daemon loads ~/.aiur/config (or none) and serves the wrong project. The comment at 213-214 says the engine mirrors workflow.ex, which it does not. Legacy .aiurconfig rejection also walks up while Elixir does not. aiur_resolve_identity re-runs both walks on every call (it is called about 10 times per launch, some nested through ensure_erlang_cookie→ensure_bg_state_dir) and unconditionally resets AIUR_PROJECT_ROOT and AIUR_PROJECT_ROOT_SOURCE. That undoes the record adoption in run_control_rpc_dispatch when the adopted identity is prepared a second time.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the project root once in the launcher, then either cd the pane to it or pass the resolved config path to the CLI (a positional config is already accepted). Alternatively, make Workflow walk up with the same $HOME stop. Compute identity once (guard with `${AIUR_PROJECT_ROOT+x}`) and add a cross-language test that runs both resolvers on the same directory tree.
